title: A yearly pilgrimage
hook: to a temple, a tree, a mountain
tomorrow: friends are the whole path. so why a poem about walking alone?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the festival calendar: a year of holy days, and a rains retreat that began with villagers worried about their crops. Today, the places those days point to.
screen: `A YEAR OF HOLY DAYS.` → `THE PLACES THEY POINT TO.`

segments.voice: People cross oceans to stand in a stadium where a band once played, or outside the house where a grandmother raised them. Ông, Mai's grandfather, wants her to visit the temple he walked into when he first came to this country. It's across town from her summer program. Here's the strange part: the Buddha sent people on trips like that too. In the long sutta of his last days, Ananda is worried. While the Buddha lives, monks come from everywhere to see him. After he's gone, who will they come to see? And the teacher who spent his life saying everything passes, don't cling, answers by giving directions.
screen: `A STADIUM, A GRANDMOTHER'S HOUSE.` → `ÔNG'S FIRST TEMPLE HERE.` → `A TEACHER OF LETTING GO, GIVING DIRECTIONS.`

segments.voice: He names four places. Where the Tathagata was born. Where he woke up. Where he first set the wheel of the teaching turning. Where he passed away. A person of faith, he says, should go and see them. So why would a teacher of letting go point at ground? Look at how the sutta describes them: places that stir samvega, a jolt of awe and urgency. Not places that hand out blessings. Places that wake you up. At the birthplace you remember he was a child once, like anyone. Where he awoke, that it can be done. Where he first taught, that it was meant to be shared. Where he died, that even he died. Every one of them points back at the teaching, not at the dirt. That's why Buddhists still travel to Lumbini, Bodh Gaya, Sarnath and Kushinagar, the places tradition matches to those four, walking around the shrines and leaving flowers. And it's why a smaller trip counts too: a temple, a tree, a mountain, a temple across town where a young man, new to a country, first found his footing. The ground doesn't do the work. It reminds you to.
screen: `FOUR PLACES, NAMED BEFORE HE DIED.` · `SAMVEGA: A JOLT OF AWE.` · `EACH ONE POINTS BACK AT THE TEACHING.` · `A TEMPLE, A TREE, A MOUNTAIN.` · then, large: `A PLACE TO GO.`

segments.voice: Pick one place you could go on purpose this year: a temple, a tree, a hill, a grave, a kitchen where someone taught you something. Ask yourself what you want it to remind you of, what usually gets in the way, and one plan to get there, a date, a ride, who comes along. Then rest with that place in mind while the sit runs.
A yearly pilgrimage: a trip made on purpose, to a place that wakes up what you already know.
Your line: a place to go. The ground reminds you, and you do the walking. That's thirteen days into the block.

screen: `DAY 1738 COUNTS.` → `A LIFE OF PRACTICE · 13 OF 45.` → `TOMORROW: FRIENDS ARE THE WHOLE PATH. SO WHY A POEM ABOUT WALKING ALONE?`

howItsDone: Buddhists from many countries travel to the places tradition links to the Buddha's birth, awakening, first teaching and passing (Lumbini, Bodh Gaya, Sarnath, Kushinagar), and also make smaller trips to temples, stupas, sacred trees and mountains, walking around shrines and offering flowers.

fork.reveal: the Buddha named the places so people would be stirred to remember: it can be done, it was shared, even he died. they point back at the teaching.

chat.meaning: Before he died, the Buddha named four places worth visiting because they stir awe and urgency, pointing back to the teaching, not handing out blessings.

tie.story: Ananda worried no one would come to see the Buddha after he died, so the Buddha named four places worth going to.

Ananda.meaning: the Buddha's cousin and close attendant

Tathagata.meaning: a title the Buddha used for himself

samvega.meaning: a jolt of awe and urgency that wakes you up

Bodh Gaya.meaning: the place tradition links to the Buddha's awakening

Kushinagar.meaning: the place tradition links to the Buddha's passing

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 16 (Mahaparinibbana Sutta) 5.8 (the four places that stir samvega)

notes: DN 16 5.8 is paraphrased: Ananda says that monks used to come to see the Buddha and asks what happens after; the Buddha names four places a person of faith should see, describing them as samvejaniya (arousing samvega). The rendering 'a jolt of awe and urgency' for samvega is an interpretive gloss; confirm. The count 'four' is the text's own.
The modern names Lumbini, Bodh Gaya, Sarnath (Isipatana) and Kushinagar are framed as 'the places tradition matches to those four'; confirm wording.

The readings 'he was a child once / it can be done / it was meant to be shared / even he died' are this lesson's reading of why each place stirs samvega, not quoted from the sutta; confirm they don't overstate.

Shape: puzzle (why does a teacher of letting go point at places?). Mai's storyline (at her summer program, see day 1737's note): Ông asks her to visit the temple he first walked into when he came to this country, across town from the program.
Surprising fact: the Buddha himself named places worth visiting after his death (DN 16).
